Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- While all eyes seem to be on "Slumdog Millionaire" for the Oscars, one very courageous little girl will be focused on another India-based film at the ceremony. Pinki, like millions in developing countries, had to live with her deformity and suffer the social consequences. It's called "Smile Pinki," and it's up for an Oscar, too -- nominated for best short documentary, which it won on Sunday. The little girl watching it from inside the Oscar ceremony has traveled all the way to Los Angeles, California, from her small Indian village with her dad -- and it has been an incredible journey for Pinki Sonkar. "Smile Pinki" tells the story of her transformation from a sad outcast to a vibrant 8-year-old with plenty of spunk. Pinki was born with a cleft lip, and her impoverished family did not have the money for corrective surgery. Like millions of other children born with the lip deformity in developing countries, Pinki simply had to live with it and suffer the social consequences. Her father Rajendra Sonkar says: "She used to go to school and the kids would not befriend her. She would say, 'I don't want to go to school.'"  Watch how Pinki was transformed by the operation » . "Pinki was a depressed, sad, lonely, shy, young little girl, growing up on the periphery of the society in a little village," said Satish Kalra, director of Smile Train's South Asian region, after meeting with Pinki. The little girl's own family was ashamed of her, Kalra says. But all of that has changed. Pinki is now a real pistol, full of energy and confidence, and she has a fantastic smile too -- thanks to the Smile Train charity. Smile Train teaches doctors in their own countries to operate on cleft lips, a deformity afflicting up to four million children across the world. iReport: Share your Oscar predictions . Pinki just happened to be one of the chosen candidates for surgery and was also chosen to be the subject of the documentary. The film chronicles her transformation, following her from her village to the hospital and home again. "She has absolutely and totally changed," said Pinki's surgeon, Dr. Subodh Kumar. The film's director is Megan Mylan. She has won several awards but not an Oscar -- until now. For Pinki and her dad, being able to see the film's director win an Oscar would be a thrill. But they know they already have the greatest prize: Pinki's new smile. "I am so happy that my daughter's lips have been repaired," her dad Rajendra said with a smile, expressing hope that the movie will inspire people to help children whose families can't afford the surgery.

(CNN) — Although “Slumdog Millionaire” has dominated much of the Oscar attention, a brave young girl was watching another film set in India. “Smile Pinki,” which follows her life-changing experience, was nominated for best documentary short—and won the Academy Award on Sunday.

Pinki Sonkar traveled with her father from their tiny village in India to Los Angeles, California, to attend the ceremony, marking the latest stage in an extraordinary journey. The documentary traces her development from an unhappy, isolated child into a spirited and confident 8-year-old.

Born with a cleft lip, Pinki could not receive corrective surgery because her family was too poor to pay for it. As happens to millions of children with the same condition in developing nations, she was forced to endure both the physical difference and the resulting social rejection.

Her father, Rajendra Sonkar, recalled that other children refused to make friends with her at school. Pinki would tell him that she no longer wanted to attend.

After meeting her, Satish Kalra, who directs Smile Train’s South Asia region, described Pinki as a lonely, withdrawn and deeply unhappy young girl living on the margins of village society. According to Kalra, even members of her own family felt ashamed of her.

That situation has now been completely reversed. Following surgery, Pinki has become lively, self-assured and energetic, with a remarkable new smile. Her treatment was made possible by Smile Train, a charity that trains doctors to perform cleft-lip operations within their own countries. The condition affects as many as four million children worldwide.

Pinki was selected both to undergo the procedure and to appear in the documentary. The film follows her from her village to the hospital, through her operation and eventually back home.

Her surgeon, Dr. Subodh Kumar, said the change in Pinki was total.

The documentary was directed by Megan Mylan, who had received several honors before but had never won an Academy Award. For Pinki and her father, seeing Mylan receive the Oscar was an exciting prospect. Still, they believed they had already received the most valuable reward of all: Pinki’s restored smile.

Rajendra said he was delighted that his daughter’s lip had been repaired. He also expressed hope that the film would encourage others to support children whose families cannot afford the operation.

# A simple surgery — and a new smile — transformed Pinki Sonkar’s life

**MIRZAPUR, India** — For the first years of her life, Pinki Sonkar lived with a cleft lip that affected far more than her appearance.

Growing up in a poor village in India’s northern state of Uttar Pradesh, Pinki faced stares and teasing and was initially unable to attend school like other children. Her family could not afford the operation needed to repair the congenital condition.

Then a social worker arrived with life-changing news: Pinki could receive surgery free of charge.

Her journey became the heart of **“Smile Pinki,”** filmmaker Megan Mylan’s intimate portrait of a child seeking treatment at a hospital in Varanasi. The film won the Academy Award for best documentary short subject in 2009, turning Pinki into an international symbol of the difference accessible medical care can make.

## A condition with social consequences

A cleft lip develops before birth when tissue forming the upper lip does not join completely. Some children also have a cleft palate, an opening in the roof of the mouth. Without treatment, clefts can contribute to difficulties with feeding, speech, hearing and dental development.

In Pinki’s community, the visible difference also brought stigma and isolation.

The documentary shows her family’s uncertainty giving way to hope after they learn about a charitable cleft-treatment program. Pinki travels to Varanasi, where surgeon Dr. Subodh Kumar Singh and his medical team repair her lip through a program supported by the nonprofit Smile Train.

The operation itself is relatively short, but its effects are profound.

## Life after surgery

After the procedure, Pinki returns home with a reconstructed lip — and with new confidence. She is able to go to school, play more freely with other children and take part in community life without the same level of ridicule that had marked her early childhood.

Her transformation is not presented simply as a cosmetic change. “Smile Pinki” illustrates how cleft surgery can alter a child’s opportunities, affecting education, relationships and self-esteem.

When the film won an Oscar, Pinki traveled to Los Angeles and appeared onstage during the Academy Awards ceremony. The girl once pushed to the margins of village life was suddenly standing before a global audience.

Pinki later became an advocate for cleft treatment, lending her story to efforts aimed at helping families understand that the condition is treatable. In 2013, she took part in a ceremonial coin toss before a Wimbledon men’s singles match, another moment that drew attention to children born with clefts.

Her story also underscored a broader reality: For many families, the greatest obstacle is not the availability of surgery but the cost of care, distance from specialist hospitals and lack of information.

“Smile Pinki” captured one child’s medical journey. But its lasting message was larger — that a straightforward operation, when made accessible, can do more than repair a lip. It can open the door to school, acceptance and a future once thought out of reach.

## ‘Smile Pinki’ Oscar Win Highlights Life-Changing Cleft Care in India

**LOS ANGELES/VARANASI —** The documentary *Smile Pinki*, which follows a young Indian girl receiving surgery for a cleft lip, won the Academy Award for Best Documentary Short Subject at the 81st Academy Awards in 2009, bringing international attention to children living with untreated clefts.

Directed by American filmmaker **Megan Mylan**, the 39-minute film tells the story of **Pinki Sonkar**, a girl from a poor rural family in Uttar Pradesh. Born with a cleft lip, Pinki faced isolation and was unable to attend school. Her life changed after a social worker identified her and helped arrange free corrective surgery.

The operation was performed by Indian surgeon **Dr. Subodh Kumar Singh** with support from **Smile Train**, an international charity focused on cleft care. The documentary follows Pinki and her family from their village to the hospital in Varanasi, showing both the medical procedure and its social impact.

Accepting the Oscar, Mylan praised Pinki and the medical workers whose efforts made the story possible. Pinki attended the Academy Awards ceremony, becoming a symbol of the many children worldwide who lack access to cleft treatment.

Smile Train works through a locally led model, providing funding, training and resources to medical professionals in countries where cleft care may otherwise be unavailable or unaffordable. In addition to surgery, its programs can include nutritional support, dental and orthodontic treatment, speech therapy and psychological care.

Cleft lip and cleft palate occur when parts of a baby’s lip or mouth do not fully join during pregnancy. Without treatment, children can experience difficulty eating, speaking and hearing, as well as stigma and social exclusion.

The success of *Smile Pinki* extended beyond its Oscar victory. By focusing on one child’s journey, the film helped draw global attention to a treatable condition and to the work of local surgeons, outreach workers and charities seeking to make long-term cleft care accessible.

## A New Smile, a New Life for Pinki Sonkar

For much of her early childhood, Pinki Sonkar lived on the margins of village life in rural Uttar Pradesh, India. Born with a cleft lip, she faced teasing and rejection because of her appearance. She rarely mixed with other children and did not attend school. Painfully shy, Pinki often hid her face and stayed close to home.

Her life changed when a local social worker learned that her condition could be corrected through a free operation. Pinki was taken to surgeon Dr. Subodh Kumar Singh, who repaired her cleft lip as part of a charitable surgical program.

The procedure transformed far more than Pinki’s appearance. Once she had recovered, she became increasingly comfortable around other people. The child who had once avoided attention began smiling openly, making friends and joining in games. She was also able to attend school and take part in activities that had previously seemed out of reach.

By the age of eight, Pinki had grown into a noticeably more confident and outgoing child. Her new self-assurance was visible in the way she spoke, laughed and interacted with others. Corrective surgery did not change who she was; it removed a barrier that had caused her to be unfairly excluded.

Pinki’s journey was documented in the short film *Smile Pinki*, which won the 2009 Academy Award for Best Documentary Short Subject. Her story drew international attention to cleft conditions and showed how access to a relatively straightforward operation can profoundly affect a child’s health, education and place within the community.

For Pinki, the surgery offered more than a repaired smile. It gave her the opportunity to be seen not for her condition, but for the lively, confident child she had always had the potential to become.

## Oscar victory puts India’s “Smile Pinki” in the spotlight

**MIRZAPUR, India —** Eight-year-old Pinki Sonkar returned to India as an unlikely symbol of hope after *Smile Pinki*, the film documenting her life-changing cleft-lip surgery, won the Academy Award for best documentary short subject at the 81st Academy Awards in February 2009.

Directed by American filmmaker Megan Mylan, the 39-minute documentary follows Pinki from her rural village in Uttar Pradesh to a hospital in Varanasi, where she receives free reconstructive surgery. The film also follows another child, Ghutaru, whose cleft had similarly limited his ability to attend school and participate fully in village life.

Pinki traveled to Los Angeles for the ceremony and joined Mylan onstage when the Oscar was presented. Accepting the award, Mylan called the children featured in the film “our stars” and said their courage had inspired the documentary.

Back in India, Pinki’s father, Rajendra Sonkar, said the family was overwhelmed by the attention and proud that his daughter’s story had reached an international audience. He described the Oscar trip and victory as something the family, which lived in difficult economic circumstances, could never have imagined.

The operation was performed by plastic surgeon Dr. Subodh Kumar Singh at the G.S. Memorial Plastic Surgery Hospital in Varanasi. Singh said the award belonged not only to the filmmakers but also to children with clefts and the medical teams working to treat them. He emphasized that a relatively short operation can dramatically change a child’s ability to eat, speak, attend school and live without social exclusion.

The surgery was supported by Smile Train, an international charity that funds cleft treatment through partnerships with local hospitals and surgeons. Smile Train representatives said Pinki’s story gave a human face to a common and treatable condition, while drawing attention to the many children who still lacked access to care.

The organization stressed that Pinki was not an isolated case: thousands of children in India were born with clefts each year, and poverty, distance from medical centers and lack of information often prevented families from seeking treatment.

For Pinki’s village, the Oscar brought television crews, visitors and celebrations. But the larger message of *Smile Pinki* remained simple: surgery did more than repair a cleft. It allowed a once-isolated child to smile openly, return to school and face her community with new confidence.
